evidence.title: Inflammatory Bowel Competitive Landscape Analysis 2026 | Eureka
evidence.text: Notably, 2025-2026 has produced an exceptional wave of approvals including Janssen’s oral peptide IL-23 antagonist Icotrokinra (March 2026), Lilly’s Mirikizumab (Omvoh) for Crohn’s expansion, and multiple Chinese-developed JAK and IL-23 mAb approvals. Specifically, the late-stage IBD landscape is bifurcated between injectable biologics — AbbVie’s Skyrizi (Risankizumab) and Rinvoq (Upadacitinib), Janssen’s Stelara (Ustekinumab) and Tremfya (Guselkumab), Takeda’s Entyvio (Vedolizumab), Pfizer’s Etrasimod (Velsipity), and BMS’s Zeposia (Ozanimod) — and the emerging oral biologic and JAK1-selective wave. Moreover, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) modulators have established a third oral mechanism alongside JAK and TYK2 inhibitors. However, the strategic outlook is increasingly defined by oral peptide IL-23 antagonists and selective JAK1 inhibitors rather than next-generation TNF or anti-integrin biologics. ... Furthermore, microbiome therapeutics, mesenchymal stem cell therapy, and IL-23 / TL1A combination biology extend the long-term modality horizon. ... Across the 200 sampled IBD programs, small molecules dominate with 114 entries (oral JAK, TYK2, S1P modulators), followed by 31 monoclonal antibodies, 6 herbal medicines, 4 mesenchymal stem cell therapies, 3 synthetic peptides, 3 cyclic peptides, 3 bispecific antibodies, 3 probiotics, and 3 polymers. Notably, the strong small-molecule presence reflects oral therapy ambitions across multiple mechanisms.

evidence.title: Competitor Landscape
evidence.text: The regulatory approval of next-generation biologics targeting novel inflammatory pathways - including JAK inhibitors, integrin antagonists, and S1P receptor modulators - has substantially broadened the therapeutic arsenal. ... The therapeutic landscape for inflammatory bowel disease has undergone revolutionary transformation through emergence of mechanistically distinct biologic classes offering superior efficacy and safety profiles compared to conventional small-molecule immunosuppressants. JAK-STAT inhibitors including tofacitinib and upadacitinib demonstrate oral bioavailability combined with targeted intracellular signaling inhibition, achieving clinical remission rates of 48-56% in moderate-to-severe disease compared to 22-28% with conventional therapies. Integrin antagonists such as vedolizumab provide selective gut-homing lymphocyte targeting, substantially reducing systemic immunosuppression and opportunistic infection risk. Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators represent an emerging frontier, with ozanimod demonstrating 41% remission rates while preserving systemic immunity. Furthermore, dual-mechanism agents combining TNF inhibition with IL-23 pathway targeting are entering late-stage development, with interim data suggesting remission rates exceeding 58-62% in treatment-naive cohorts. ... Biologic therapies including TNF inhibitors, integrin antagonists, IL-12/IL-23 inhibitors, and JAK inhibitors represent the most rapidly expanding therapeutic category, driven by superior efficacy profiles enabling disease remission in 45-65% of patients compared to 20-35% with conventional small-molecule therapies. ... Integrin antagonist vedolizumab commands 18.7% of biologic market revenues, offering gut-selective targeting advantages particularly appealing to patients with treatment-limiting infections or malignancy concerns. ... Patients presenting with pure colonic ulcerative colitis frequently receive integrin antagonists or JAK inhibitors as first-line biologic therapy, leveraging gut-selective mechanisms minimizing systemic immunosuppression.

Most adverse events were mild or moderate. The most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse events (in ≥5% of in any treatment group) were upper respiratory tract infection (six [9%] of 70 patients in the tamuzimod 60 mg group, one [1%] of 73 in the tamuzimod 30 mg group, and one [1%] of 70 in the placebo group), anaemia (three [3%], four [5%], and six [9%]), and headache (four [6%], five [7%], and two [3%]). The overall safety profile was favourable and consistent with that of guselkumab in approved indications. In the induction study, adverse events were reported by 49% of patients in both groups (208 of 421 guselkumab-treated patients and 138 of 280 placebo-treated patients), serious adverse events were reported by 3% (12 of 421) of guselkumab-treated patients and 7% (20 of 280) of placebo-treated patients, and adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were reported by 2% (seven of 421) of guselkumab-treated patients and 4% (11 of 280) of placebo-treated patients. In the maintenance study, adverse event rates were similar among groups, and the most frequently reported adverse events in all groups were ulcerative colitis, COVID-19, and arthralgia. No active tuberculosis, anaphylaxis, serum sickness, or clinically important hepatic disorders were reported in either study.INTERPRETATIONGuselkumab was effective and safe as induction and maintenance therapy in patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis.FUNDINGJanssen Research and Development.

evidence.title: Antispasmodics and IBD
evidence.text: Antispasmodics suppress muscle spasms, helping to reduce stomach pain, cramping and bloating. They are sometimes used in IBD to relieve symptoms. ... Antispasmodic medicines are a type of symptomatic medicine, which suppress muscle spasms. They are used to help ease symptoms such as functional abdominal pain, cramping and bloating you may have as a result of a wide range of conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). They can also help to reduce the movement (motility) of your gut. ... People who have IBD, such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, may be advised to take antispasmodic medicines to help to ease pain, discomfort and symptoms whilst other medicines take effect, or if they have symptoms that are not responding to other IBD medicines. ... There are two main types of antispasmodics, antimuscarinics (also called anticholinergics) and smooth muscle relaxants. ... As mentioned earlier, your body sends chemical messages to your gut, telling the muscles to contract. Antimuscarinics block the action of the chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) acetylcholine, reducing the strength of muscle contractions, spasms and cramps. This also reduces gut motility. Examples include: - Dicyclomine (Bentyl) - Hyoscyamine - Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) - Atropine - Propantheline ... Smooth muscle relaxants work directly on the smooth muscle wall of the gut, helping it to relax and relieving pain associated with contractions, cramps and spasms. Examples include: - Mebeverine (Colofac, Duspamen and Duspatalin) - Alverine citrate (Spasmonal) ... Smooth muscle relaxants tend to have fewer side effects so will often be suggested first. Some people seem to respond better to one type of antispasmodic than to another, so if one type does not work for you, it may be worth trying another. ... It is generally recommended that you only take antispasmodics when necessary, stopping if the symptoms settle down. ... Generally smooth muscle relaxant antispasmodics will have fewer, milder side effects than antimuscarinics. ... This will be listed in the patient information leaflets, and includes: - If you have, or might have a bowel obstruction - If you already have gut motility issues - If you have myasthenia gravis, a condition that causes muscle weakness

output.summarized_answer: Dicyclomine (Bentyl; dicyclomine hydrochloride; dicycloverine) is an anticholinergic/antimuscarinic antispasmodic. Antimuscarinics block acetylcholine, reducing gut contractions and motility; anticholinergic/antimuscarinic agents also inhibit GI smooth-muscle contraction partly by blocking calcium transport and decrease colonic motility. Antimuscarinic agents named alongside it are hyoscyamine (hyoscyamine sulfate), hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan), atropine, propantheline (propantheline bromide; PRO-BANTHINE), cimetropium bromide, otilanium bromide, octylonium bromide, prifinium bromide and darifenacin. Propantheline is also identified as a synthetic, nonselective muscarinic receptor antagonist. Antispasmodics are used for IBD symptoms including pain, cramping and bloating; the American Gastroenterological Association is said to recommend them for IBD patients with IBS or functional symptoms. Hyoscyamine and dicyclomine are identified as frequently used for pain associated with IBD inflammation or partial obstruction; one review calls hyoscine (hyoscyamine) the most efficacious of the medications studied by that group and the only one available in US markets, while also stating that definitive evidence supporting antispasmodic use in IBD is lacking. [E1][E2][E3][E5] A separate review identifies hyoscine as scopolamine and as anticholinergic/antimuscarinic; it reports three studies in which hyoscine taken for 4 weeks to 3 months was more efficacious than placebo for IBS symptoms. [E4] For dicyclomine, two randomized, placebo-controlled IBS studies found symptom improvement versus placebo; one found no difference in adverse-event rates, while the other reported adverse events in 69% with dicyclomine 160 mg/d continuously for 2 weeks versus 16% with placebo. The dicyclomine and hyoscine studies reviewed were published in 1990 or earlier and used different doses, treatment durations and outcome assessments. [E4] In an IBD cohort of 85,859 patients (median age 50; 53.8% female), 5,661 used antispasmodics; use was defined as a prescription for dicyclomine or hyoscyamine with at least a 30-day supply. Antispasmodic use was associated with higher rates of abdominal pain and opioid use (P < 0.001), including higher abdominal-pain rates at 1 month and, among opioid-naïve patients, opioid use of 1.1% versus 0.2% at follow-up (P < 0.001). Use was also associated with corticosteroid use, clinic and ER visits, and hospitalization; it was not associated with improvement in abdominal pain or opioid use, including after adjustment for IBD severity and baseline characteristics. [E5]

Dekavil (F8-IL-10; PF-06687234) is a fully human F8 antibody-fragment–IL-10 fusion protein: F8 binds fibronectin EDA, and the product is designed to enrich IL-10 delivery to inflamed tissue. Pfizer exclusively in-licensed F8IL10 from Philogen for development in inflammatory disorders. In the Phase 2A BUILD UC study, NCT03269695, participants with active UC who were not in remission on infliximab received subcutaneous PF-06687234 20 mg weekly or placebo while continuing intravenous infliximab every 6 or 8 weeks for 12 weeks. Johnson & Johnson’s investigational antibody combo failed to significantly improve remission and response in a pair of mid-stage trials of inflammatory bowel diseases, but that isn’t stopping the pharma from forging ahead to pivotal testing. The investigational co-antibody therapy, dubbed JNJ-4804, is a fixed-dose combination of the pharma’s anti-IL-23 therapy Tremfya and TNF-alpha blocker Simponi. Combining both molecules in one therapy “yields a synergistic therapeutic approach” for patients resistant to monotherapies, Esi Lamousé Smith, vice president of J&J’s Gastroenterology Disease Area, said in a Tuesday release. ... In the Phase 2b DUET-CD study, high-dose JNJ-4804 showed significantly higher clinical remission and endoscopic response rates versus monotherapy with Simponi, but not versus Tremfya. ... output.summarized_answer: JNJ-4804 (also JNJ-78934804) is a fixed-dose co-antibody combination of guselkumab and golimumab, targeting IL-23 and TNF-α in one subcutaneous injection. Johnson & Johnson calls it the first and only fixed-dose co-antibody designed for molecular synergy in IBD; the combination’s preclinical rationale is complementary and distinct IL-23 and TNF-α activity, with molecular synergy demonstrated in VEGA. [E1][E4][E9][E10] In Phase 2b DUET-CD (NCT05242471) and DUET-UC (NCT05242484), JNJ-4804 was evaluated in moderately to severely active, systemically refractory Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. The studies compared it with placebo and the component monotherapies; the company describes them as randomized, double-blind, dose-ranging studies. DUET-CD included low-, mid- and high-dose JNJ-4804 arms; Healio reports 693 randomized adults, 57% men, assigned to guselkumab, golimumab, those three JNJ-4804 dose levels or placebo. [E4][E3][E9][E10] In DUET-CD, Healio reports high-dose JNJ-4804 differences versus golimumab of 25.7 for clinical remission (P<.001) and 18.5 for endoscopic response (nominal P<.001). At week 48, it reports differences for clinical remission and endoscopic response, respectively, of 27.3 and 21.2 versus golimumab, 21.2 and 11.7 versus guselkumab, and 39.4 and 35 versus placebo; it also reports no increased adverse-event risk versus monotherapy. [E3] Johnson & Johnson reports overall-population week-48 clinical-remission and endoscopic-response rates of 50.8% and 38.1% for JNJ-4804, versus 25.4% and 19.8% for golimumab and 42.5% and 33.9% for guselkumab. It also reports clinical remission of 41.0% for JNJ-4804 versus 11.5% for golimumab and 34.0% for guselkumab; the excerpt does not identify the disease population for this second set of rates. [E1][E4][E5] For patients with Crohn’s disease refractory to two or more systemic-therapy classes, Johnson & Johnson reports clinically meaningful week-48 improvements across multiple clinical and endoscopic endpoints versus golimumab, guselkumab and placebo; its congress materials characterize high-dose results in patients refractory to two or more systemic-therapy mechanisms as exceeding the monotherapies’ additive effects across key clinical, endoscopic and histologic-endoscopic endpoints. [E1][E5][E9][E10] BioSpace says the combination did not significantly improve remission and response versus guselkumab in the mid-stage trials: in DUET-CD, high-dose JNJ-4804 was significantly higher than golimumab but not guselkumab; in DUET-UC, remission was significantly higher than golimumab but not guselkumab, while endoscopic improvement, a secondary endpoint in that study, was numerically higher versus either monotherapy. [E8] Johnson & Johnson said it would initiate Phase 3 DUET ENCORE-CD and DUET ENCORE-UC; that is a stated plan, not confirmation that either trial has started. [E4] The earlier Phase 2a VEGA study (NCT03662542) evaluated the combination in moderately to severely active UC in 214 anti-TNF-naive participants over 12 weeks. Its regimens were guselkumab 200 mg IV at weeks 0, 4 and 8; golimumab 200 mg SC at week 0 then 100 mg SC at weeks 2, 6 and 10; or combination guselkumab 200 mg IV plus golimumab 200 mg SC at week 0, golimumab 100 mg SC at weeks 2, 6 and 10, and guselkumab 200 mg IV at weeks 4 and 8. Clinical response was 44/72 (61.1%) with golimumab, 53/71 (74.6%) with guselkumab and 59/71 (83.1%) with the combination; the combination comparison had p=0.003 versus golimumab and p=0.215 versus guselkumab. Clinical remission, symptomatic remission, endoscopic improvement and normalized fecal calprotectin at week 12 were significant versus both monotherapies; endoscopic normalization was significant versus guselkumab, and histologic remission was significant versus golimumab. [E6] The named competing agents include golimumab (an anti-TNF antibody) and guselkumab (an anti-IL-23 antibody), both JNJ-associated agents used as DUET comparators and components of the combination. [E3][E4] Guselkumab is an IL-23p19-targeting human IgG1λ antibody whose Fc can target CD64 (FcγRI) on some IL-23-expressing myeloid antigen-presenting cells; the cited market overview lists approvals for PsO (2017), PsA (2020), CD (2024.09) and UC (2025.03). [E2] Other named IL-23 competitors are mirikizumab (an IL-23p19-targeting humanized IgG4 antibody, developed by Eli Lilly; UC approval 2023.10 and CD approval 2025.01) and risankizumab (identified as an IL-23 inhibitor). Named TNF-inhibitor competitors are adalimumab and infliximab. [E2][E7] The IBD clinical-trial list also names ABX464 (obefazimod), Tulisokibart (MK-7240), RHB-204, TEV-574 (duvakitug), AGMB-129, olamkicept, zotemtegrast, ATH-063, SPY001, SPY002, SPY003, DB-3Q, zasocitinib, ABBV-243, ABBV-701, TRX103 and XmAb412. [E7] Johnson & Johnson’s stated plan for Phase 3 advancement is the available later-stage plan; the supplied information does not establish subsequent trial initiation. [E4]

Early disease patients also experienced significantly fewer serious adverse events. ... SOR102 is an oral bispecific antibody targeting TNF and IL-23p19 developed for ulcer ative colitis. This phase 1, double blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated its safety, pharmacokinetics, and preliminary efficacy in healthy participants and patients with active ulcerative colitis. Across single and multiple ascending doses, SOR102 was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events and no clinically significant safety signals. In patients with ulcerative colitis treated for 42 days, clinical responses were more frequent with SOR102 than placebo, particularly with twice-daily dosing. Symptomatic remission was achieved in over half of patients receiving twice-daily SOR102, while no placebo-treated patients reached remission. Although one severe disease exacerbation occurred, it was not considered treatment related. Overall, the favourable safety profile and early signs of clinical bene fit support further clinical development of SOR102 as a potential oral therapy for ulcerative colitis.

AZD5148 (formerly PA41), which AstraZeneca is developing, is an anti-TcdB monoclonal antibody that binds the toxin’s glucosyltransferase domain (GTD) and blocks delivery of its enzymatic cargo into host cells. It has a YTE Fc substitution (M252Y/S254T/T256E) intended to extend its half-life. One study calls it a human mAb, while another calls it humanized. [E1][E3][E4][E5] Its epitope was reported as 99.58% conserved across 9,134 global isolates, versus 82.47% for bezlotoxumab, and AZD5148 neutralized eight recent circulating TcdB ribotypes in vitro. In vitro EC50 values against TcdB1 and TcdB2 were 1,000- to 14,000-fold lower than bezlotoxumab’s; in mouse CDI models AZD5148 protected against weight loss and mortality at significantly lower doses. It also protected in a gnotobiotic piglet model and in mouse models using strains with different TcdB ribotypes. Adding the anti-TcdA mAb PA50 provided no additional protective benefit in a mouse model. [E1][E3][E4][E5]

The Phase IIb PRISM study (NCT07285213) is described as evaluating AZD5148 to prevent CDI recurrence in adults aged 18 years and above with a qualifying CDI episode. It lists 230 patients, AZD5148 or placebo, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design, efficacy as the primary endpoint, and safety and pharmacokinetics as secondary endpoints; first patient/participant dosed (FPCD) was Q4 2025, and data were anticipated after 2027. [E1][E5][E7] The Phase I study (NCT06469151) in 84 healthy volunteers is described as randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose escalation, with safety as the primary endpoint and pharmacokinetic parameters as secondary endpoints. Cohort 1 received dose 1 intramuscularly (i.m.) or placebo; cohorts 2a and 2b received dose 2 i.m. or placebo, with 2b in Chinese participants; cohort 3 received dose 2 intravenously (i.v.) or placebo; cohorts 4a and 4b received dose 3 i.v. or placebo, with 4b in Chinese participants; and cohort 5 received dose 4 i.v. or placebo. FPCD was Q2 2024, last patient/participant dosed (LPCD) was Q4 2024, and data readout was listed as Q1 2026. [E7]

Ozmosi lists three Phase I trials: D8820C00005, active, not recruiting, for Clostridium infections, with a primary completion date of 2025-12-29 and a 69% probability of success; jRCT2071240071, not yet recruiting, in healthy volunteers, with a primary completion date of 2026-01-12; and D8820C00002, active, not recruiting, in healthy volunteers, with a primary completion date of 2025-11-07 and a 69% probability of success. Its profile lists AZD5148 as not approved, with no approved countries. [E6]

Bezlotoxumab (Zinplava) is an anti-TcdB mAb and the named approved comparator: it binds two epitopes in TcdB’s CROPS near the hinge region and was approved in 2016. Its stated US and EU regimen was one 10 mg/kg i.v. infusion to prevent recurrent CDI in high-risk individuals receiving antibacterial treatment; neutralizing TcdB with bezlotoxumab reduces recurrent infection and adverse outcomes. Its production was discontinued in January 2025. [E1][E2][E3][E4] Actoxumab (CDA1) is identified as an anti-TcdA mAb selected for in-vitro potency and efficacy in a lethal intoxication hamster model; the evidence does not establish it as an anti-TcdB agent. [E1]

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, is characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. This inflammation is driven, at least in part, by excessive infiltration and retention of intestinal-homing lymphocytes. An adhesion cascade drives the infiltration of immune cells. The binding of immune cell glycoproteins to their corresponding epithelial cell selectins results in partial retention and the "rolling" of immune cells along the endothelium. A stable arrest is mediated by stronger interactions between immune cell integrins and cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) on the endothelial cell; once arrested, immune cells will extravasate and enter the target tissue. ... output.summarized_answer: Vedolizumab is a marketed anti-integrin monoclonal antibody from Takeda that targets α4β7, blocking interactions with MAdCAM-1 and fibronectin; it is gut-selective and does not affect α4β1:VCAM-1 interactions. It is approved for ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease, including induction and maintenance, and is described as effective with a favorable safety profile. [E1][E2][E5] Etrolizumab (rhuMAb β7; PRO145223) is a humanized IgG1κ anti-β7 monoclonal antibody from Genentech that blocks α4β7 and αEβ7 interactions with MAdCAM-1 and E-cadherin, respectively. Reported binding affinities are 116 ± 11 pmol/L for human α4β7 and 1,800 ± 170 pmol/L for human αEβ7; reported IC50 values are 0.075 ± 0.034 nmol/L for α4β7 interactions with MAdCAM-1, 0.089 ± 0.009 nmol/L with VCAM-1, 0.119 ± 0.056 nmol/L with fibronectin, and 3.96 ± 1.78 nmol/L for αEβ7 interaction with E-cadherin. [E3][E9] A Phase 2 UC study enrolled 124 patients and found greater clinical remission with induction treatment than placebo; Phase 3 studies were reported in UC and CD, including HIBISCUS I and II, GARDENIA, LAUREL, HICKORY and BERGAMOT, with open-label extensions COTTONWOOD (UC) and JUNIPER (CD). [E2][E4] Etrolizumab was also reported to internalize α4β7, impair adhesion to MAdCAM-1, and produce greater α4β7 internalization than vedolizumab; mouse models and genetic analyses were reported to show reduced accumulation of cytotoxic intraepithelial lymphocytes and inflammatory CD8+ T cells in intestinal mucosa in CD. [E6][E8] Abrilumab (AMG181; MEDI7183) is a fully human anti-α4β7 monoclonal antibody; the evidence lists Amgen and AstraZeneca and Phase 2b. In a randomized, double-blind, multicenter study in moderate-to-severe UC refractory to anti-TNF or immunomodulator therapy, it showed evidence of efficacy and an acceptable safety profile, with no reported PML cases. In moderate-to-severe CD, the Phase 2b primary endpoint—CDAI remission (score <150) at week 8—was not met. [E1] Other named IBD agents provide mechanistic contrasts: tofacitinib is an oral small molecule inhibiting JAK 1 and 3, and JAK 2 at higher doses, and underwent Phase 2 and 3 studies in UC. [E4] Etrolizumab Phase 3 studies included a head-to-head comparison against adalimumab. [E4]

evidence.title: www.creative-biolabs.com › blog › adcHyaluronidase-Conjugated Liposomes May Effectively Target ...
evidence.text: The research team developed an efficient drug delivery system: quercetin was encapsulated into liposomes, and hyaluronidase (HAase) was conjugated to the surface of the liposomes. This novel liposome was named HQL. ... In vitro experiments showed that HQL could stably exist in 10% fetal bovine serum and plasma for 15 days. ... In vitro cell experiments demonstrated that HQL had a significant proliferation-inhibiting effect on pancreatic cancer cells (PANC-1 and Miapaca-2), with an IC50 value lower than that of quercetin and other controls. It had no obvious inhibitory effect on the proliferation of normal pancreatic ductal epithelial cells (HPNE), showing good tumor cell specificity. HQL had stronger penetration ability in HA-rich agarose gels. In 2D and 3D cell culture models, it was more effectively taken up by pancreatic cancer cells, promoted cancer cell apoptosis, and induced cell cycle arrest at the G2/M phase. In experiments with 3D-cultured PANC-1 cells and PDAC organoids, HQL also showed superior ability to inhibit cell proliferation and promote apoptosis compared to other control groups. In in vivo experiments, the researchers established a pancreatic cancer mouse model. Results showed that the tumor volume and weight in the HQL treatment group were significantly lower than those in the control group and other treatment groups, reducing tumor volume by 73% and decreasing HA levels in tumor tissues by 95%. Fluorescent labeling experiments revealed that HQL mainly accumulated in tumor tissues, with less distribution in organs such as the liver. The drug concentration of HQL in the blood could still be maintained at an effective level (50 μg/mL) within 48 hours, while the concentration of orally administered quercetin dropped to below 0.2 μg/mL after 48 hours. Furthermore, the in vivo enzymatic activity of HQL peaked at 60 U/mL at 2 hours, then gradually decreased and remained at approximately 20 U/mL within 48 hours. Safety evaluation indicated that HQL had no obvious impact on mouse body weight or the morphology and function of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney), showing no potential toxic side effects. Mechanistic studies found that HQL may exert its effects of inhibiting tumor cell growth and promoting apoptosis by downregulating the expression of cell cycle-related proteins (CCNB1, CDK1, and PLK1) as well as apoptosis-related factors PI3K/AKT and Bcl-2. In summary, the HQL liposomal drug delivery system developed in this study can effectively degrade HA in the pancreatic cancer tumor microenvironment, enhance drug penetration and delivery efficiency, significantly inhibit pancreatic cancer growth, and has good safety. It provides a new and promising drug delivery method for the adjuvant treatment of pancreatic cancer, which is expected to bring new hope to pancreatic cancer patients in the future and promote further development in the field of pancreatic cancer treatment.

evidence.title: An efficient drug delivery system to block pancreatic cancer
evidence.text: Hence, we developed an efficient drug delivery system by encapsulation of Que. into liposomes and conjugation with hyaluronidase (HAase) at liposome surface, termed as HQL. In the presence of HAase, HQL were predominantly accumulated at tumor with enhanced permeability and retention effect. Treatment of xenografted tumor mice with HQL gave rise to suppressed tumor growth, while no toxic effects were observed in mice. HQL demonstrated the strong ability to inhibit cell proliferation, promote cell apoptosis, and induce arrest at G2/M cell cycle in pancreatic cancer lines, three-dimensional cultured cell spheroids and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)-derived organoids. Mechanistically, HQL downregulated expression of cell cycle-associated protein (CCNB1, CDK1 and PLK1) and cell apoptosis-associated factors PI3K/AKT and Bcl-2. In summary, HQL degraded HA in the tumor microenvironment to enhance nano-particle penetration and inhibited tumor cell growth, eliciting efficacy of anti-tumor therapy. Thereof, HQL may provide a novel efficient drug delivery approach for the adjuvant treatment of pancreatic cancer.

evidence.text: **Abstract:** Despite the success of monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapies in treating inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a persistent therapeutic ceiling remains. This comprehensive review explores emerging strategies to enhance the efficacy of mAb-based treatments. Key among these is the development of bispecific antibodies designed to simultaneously engage two cytokine targets, offering dual blockade of inflammatory pathways and the potential for synergistic effects. Co-formulation approaches, comprising two or more mAbs within a single therapeutic product, are also examined as a means of broadening immunologic coverage and streamlining delivery. Finally, advances in pharmacokinetic optimisation are discussed, including Fc region modifications, polyethylene glycol conjugation, albumin fusion, and glycoengineering, all aimed at reducing immunogenicity and extending half-life. ... ### Modifying the Fc Region ... ^22,23^ There are no current afucosylated mAbs licenced for IBD or immune mediated inflammatory disorders (IMIDs) but given the feasibility of the technology and the demonstrated impact upon NK cells via enhanced ADCC activity, it remains an area of interest. ... Seres has obtained FDA Fast Track designation for SER-287 in active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis. SER-287 targets restructuring the microbiome to reduce proinflammatory activity and modulate UC-relevant inflammatory pathways, potentially providing a much-needed non-immunosuppressive treatment option to patients suffering from ulcerative colitis. SER-287 has the potential to be used as both a monotherapy and in combination with other approved agents. The SER-287 Phase 2b ECO-RESET study is a randomized, placebo-controlled, three-arm induction trial that has enrolled 203 patients with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis who have had inadequate response or loss of response on prior therapy. In arm A, patients receive a short course of vancomycin preconditioning followed by ten weeks of the same daily regimen used in the arm of the Phase 1b trial that showed the highest clinical remission rate. In arm B, patients receive vancomycin preconditioning followed by two weeks of the SER-287 daily regimen as in the first arm, followed by eight weeks of a lower dose of SER-287. In arm C, patients receive placebo. The study’s primary endpoint is the proportion of patients achieving clinical remission at ten weeks. The study will assess endoscopic improvement as a secondary endpoint, as well as a range of microbiome and metabolomic measures. Seres has completed enrollment in the SER-287 Phase 2b ECO-RESET induction study in patients with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis and expects to report topline clinical study results in mid-2021, with additional microbiome biomarker data becoming available in H2 2021. ... evidence.text: Phase II trials have been completed for ankylosing spondylitis (“AS”), with additional trials ongoing or planned for ulcerative colitis (“UC”), atopic dermatitis (“AD”), psoriatic arthritis (“PsA”), Crohn’s disease (“CD”), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (“COPD”). ... Hemay007 is screened from a compound library directed by multiple pharmacological functional substructures and is a TNF-�small molecule regulator. In the spontaneous UC monkey model, Hemay007 reduced the number of ulcers in the colons of the testing subjects, and pathological examinations of the intestines after treatment revealed that the colon tissue almost returned to a normal state. As of the Latest Practicable Date, we have completed the Phase II clinical trial for monotherapy for UC. A Phase II clinical trial for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is ongoing. For phase II clinical trial of Hemay007 for UC at week 12, clinical response rates, as evaluated by both central laboratory and principal investigator (PI) assessments, there was no statistically significant differences across all groups in both the FAS and PPS populations (P > 0.05 for all comparisons). Clinical remission rates at Week 12 were also comparable among the treatment and placebo groups, with no statistically significant differences observed. For the development of Hemay007, we will prioritize the clinical trial for RA. Currently, we do not have a definitive timetable for the next steps in UC.

ClinicalTrials.gov had no efficacy or safety results posted. Emvistegrast (GS-1427) is an oral α4β7 integrin inhibitor developed by Gilead Sciences. Its Phase 2 study, NCT06290934 (SWIFT), evaluates three doses against placebo over 76 weeks; the week-12 primary endpoint is clinical response, defined as a decrease in modified Mayo score of at least 2 points and 30% from baseline, with improved rectal bleeding score. Eligibility includes adults aged 18–75 with moderately to severely active UC, endoscopic and histologic confirmation, disease extent of at least 15 cm from the anal verge, modified Mayo score 5–9 and endoscopic subscore at least 2, with inadequate response or intolerance to prior treatments including corticosteroids, immunomodulators or advanced therapies. Exclusions include Crohn’s disease, toxic megacolon, prior vedolizumab exposure and contraindicated medications. The pipeline review lists primary completion in October 2025 and final completion in February 2027. LARVOL lists enrollment/status and timing revisions: one entry gives 228 participants and active, not recruiting, with completion changed from July 2027 to April 2028; another gives 228 participants, recruiting, with enrollment changed from 423, completion from March 2028 to February 2027, primary completion from May 2027 to October 2025, and status from not yet recruiting to recruiting. A healthy-participant study assessed tablet versus capsule bioavailability and food and omeprazole effects on exposure; all adverse events were grade 1, with no serious adverse events or deaths. Induction-phase efficacy and safety results for the Phase 2 SWIFT trial are identified for UEGW 2026, with the full abstract slated for presentation day. [E2][E3][E6][E7]

Other UC agents named in the evidence include the following. The α4β7-targeting agents PTG-100, an oral antagonist peptide, and PN-943, an oral gastrointestinal-restricted cyclic peptide, were Phase 2b (NCT02895100) and Phase 2 (NCT04504383), respectively; PTG-100 was terminated early for futility in March 2018, while PN-943 completed in February 2023 and did not meet the primary endpoint at the 450 mg dose. [E1][E2] Abrilumab is a human monoclonal IgG2 antibody targeting α4β7, studied in Phase 2b trials NCT01694485 and NCT01959165; the global study completed, with remission of 13.3% at 70 mg versus 4.3% with placebo. Vatelizumab (SAR339658) is a monoclonal antibody targeting α4β7, studied in Phase 2 trials NCT01659138 and NCT01861249, which were terminated early due to recruitment challenges. [E1][E2]

MORF-057 is an oral small-molecule α4β7 inhibitor; EMERALD-1 (NCT05291689) was Phase 2a and completed in November 2023, and EMERALD-2 (NCT05611671) was Phase 2b with primary completion in November 2024. [E1][E2] Carotegrast methyl (AJM300) is an oral small-molecule α4-integrin antagonist, rather than an α4β7-specific agent; its Phase 3 study NCT03531892 enrolled 203 people with moderately active UC and tested 960 mg three times daily versus placebo for 8 weeks. The review table gives clinical response of 45% versus 21% at week 8, while its narrative gives 46% versus 21%. [E3]

SPY001 is described as an investigational small molecule targeting α4β7 for moderate-to-severe UC, in Phase 2, with Spyre Therapeutics, Inc. named in the listing. Its trials are NCT07012395 and NCT07652294; the first is recruiting and the second is enrolling by invitation for long-term safety and efficacy. Both are described as randomized, double-blind and controlled, with combined enrollment of 1,290. [E4] Vedolizumab (Entyvio) is named as targeting the same clinically validated pathway as emvistegrast. The Phase 2a UC combination OD-07656 plus vedolizumab is described as an IRAK4 inhibitor plus an α4β7 antagonist, NCT06850727, started in June 2025 with estimated completion in November 2026. [E1][E5]

The review also lists UC agents outside the α4β7 class: ivarmacitinib (SHR0302), a selective JAK1 inhibitor blocking the JAK-STAT pathway, in Phase 2 (NCT03675477; completed February 2021) and Phase 3 (NCT05181137; status unknown); and brepocitinib (PF-06700841), an oral dual TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor, in Phase 2b VIBRATO (NCT02958865), completed in May 2021 and advanced to alopecia areata trials. [E1] Tulisokibart (MK-7240) is a humanized IgG1 antibody targeting TL1A, with Phase 2 and Phase 3 studies (NCT04996797 [ARTEMIS-UC], NCT06052059 and NCT06651281); Phase 2 is completed and Phase 3 is ongoing, with estimated completion in December 2029. [E1] The listed Phase 3b combination mirikizumab plus tirzepatide is an IL-23p19 antibody plus dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist, NCT06937086, started in June 2025 with estimated completion in April 2028. [E1]

output.summarized_answer: Oral ADT-1004 at 40 mg/kg caused substantial growth inhibition and profound regression of KRAS-G12D and KRAS-G12V tumors, without accompanying body-weight loss. [E1] In PDAC experiments, KRAS-G12D murine cells (KPC-luc or 2838c3-luc) were implanted orthotopically in C57BL/6J mice, and four KRAS-mutant PDAC PDX tumors were implanted subcutaneously in NSG mice; ADT-1004 inhibited tumor growth in these models. [E2][E3] ADT-1004 suppressed PDX tumors with KRAS-G12D, G12V, G12C and G13Q mutations. [E2][E3] A review instead lists G12Q among the responsive mutations. [E7] Doses of 20–50 mg/kg produced comparable statistically significant reductions in tumor weight versus vehicle or 10 mg/kg ADT-1004; oral 40 mg/kg significantly reduced tumor growth by bioluminescence imaging and tumor weight versus vehicle, without differences in body weight. [E2] In orthotopic and PDX PDAC models, daily oral ADT-1004 significantly inhibited tumor growth. [E6] In NSG mice with parental MIA PaCa-2 tumors, ADT-1004, sotorasib and adagrasib were each given at 40 mg/kg once daily, 5 times weekly; each treatment produced comparable decreases in tumor volume and final tumor weight. ADT-1004 also showed greater efficacy than sotorasib and adagrasib in resistant tumor models, including models with MRTX1133-resistant KRAS-G12D mutant cells. [E2][E3][E10] ADT-1004 did not affect growth of tumors from RAS-wild-type PDAC cells, including BxPC3; murine RAS-driven PDAC models also showed robust, durable antitumor activity at well-tolerated doses.
